title: Gulf producers stand to gain as China replaces Iranian loss
section_path: Gulf producers stand to gain as China replaces Iranian loss
section_path_text: Gulf producers stand to gain as China replaces Iranian loss
summary:
Main
The loss of Iranian crude creates an opening for Gulf producers, while China's fuel export policy is closely linked to Middle East Gulf crude availability. By Emma Li
China's non-Iranian Middle Eastern crude arrivals are set to reach their highest level since the war began, despite VLCC tightness and Hormuz ship-to-ship (STS) bottlenecks delaying cargo deliveries. As Iranian supplies dwindle, Gulf producers - particularly Saudi Arabia and Iraq - are well positioned to capture more of China's crude demand.

China's non-Iranian Middle Eastern crude arrivals are set to reach their highest level since the war began, despite VLCC tightness and Hormuz ship-to-ship (STS) bottlenecks delaying cargo deliveries.

children.title: China's Middle Eastern crude arrivals recover despite Hormuz bottlenecks
section_path: China's Middle Eastern crude arrivals recover despite Hormuz bottlenecks
children.section_path_text: China's Middle Eastern crude arrivals recover despite Hormuz bottlenecks
children.summary: Recent Middle Eastern crude arrivals into China have come entirely from the Middle East Gulf (MEG), rather than the Red Sea or Mediterranean, as China-bound loadings have shifted fully back to the MEG since late July. Although voyages from the MEG to China are taking longer because of STS transfers East of Hormuz or near India, non-Iranian Middle Eastern crude arrivals are still expected to reach around 4.5mbd in October, close to the 2025 average of 4.7mbd.

children.title: Replacing Iranian crude is critical to China's fuel balance
section_path: Replacing Iranian crude is critical to China's fuel balance
children.section_path_text: Replacing Iranian crude is critical to China's fuel balance
children.summary: China's total seaborne crude imports are expected to strengthen to around 8.8mbd in October, up from a Q3 average of 7.5mbd, although still well below the 2025 average of 10.6mbd. The loss of Iranian barrels, however, remains a major challenge for China's crude supply and refined-product balance.

children.title: China's fuel export policy remains tied to MEG crude availability
section_path: China's fuel export policy remains tied to MEG crude availability
children.section_path_text: China's fuel export policy remains tied to MEG crude availability
children.summary: China's seaborne clean fuel exports are tightly controlled by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and governed by annual quotas. Amid the Hormuz crisis, the authorities appear to be adjusting export plans more quickly in response to supply risks.

children.title: Conclusion: Gulf crude gains, but China's fuel exports remain the swing factor
section_path: Conclusion: Gulf crude gains, but China's fuel exports remain the swing factor
children.section_path_text: Conclusion: Gulf crude gains, but China's fuel exports remain the swing factor
children.summary: The loss of Iranian crude is reshaping China's import mix, creating an opportunity for Saudi Arabia and Iraq to capture additional demand as refiners seek replacement barrels. Yet stronger Gulf arrivals will not automatically translate into a recovery in China's fuel exports.
